author: claude
title: French Oak vs American Oak Chemistry

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: When winemakers talk about barrels, they often compare French oak and American oak. Do they really taste different?

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: They do. They come from different species of oak trees, and the wood has a different chemistry. French oak usually has a tighter grain, because the trees grow slowly in cooler forests.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: What does that mean for the wine?

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: French oak tends to give more subtle flavors. Gentle spice, toast, a little vanilla. And it often adds a fine, silky tannin structure.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: American oak is famous for stronger, sweeter aromas. It's rich in compounds called lactones, which can smell like coconut. It also gives clear notes of vanilla, from a compound called vanillin.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Where does vanillin come from, exactly?

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Partly from the wood itself, but also from the toast level. When a barrel is made, the inside is heated over a fire. A light toast keeps more of the natural wood character. A heavy toast creates smoky, caramel and coffee notes.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: So the winemaker can almost choose a flavor.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: To some extent, yes. That's why the choice of barrel is a serious decision. Classic Spanish Rioja often used American oak, while many Bordeaux and Burgundy producers prefer French oak.
